# njmunicipalities-api

This is the source code for the NJ Municipalities API deployed at `api.tor-gu.com`.

It contains the names and GEOID/FIPS codes for every municipality and county in NJ, from 2000 to 2026, and records the changes from year to year.

See the related [njmunicipalities data package for R](https://github.com/tor-gu/njmunicipalities) for 
more details on the underlying dataset.

## Try it out

### OpenAPI/Swagger
There is an OpenAPI/swagger document deployed [here](https://tor-gu.com/apis/njmunicipalities.html)
that you can play with.


### Sample code
Each endpoint returns paginated results, with a `"next"` url in the `"links"` section 
indicating that there are more results to be retrieved.

This is illustrated in the python code below, which loads the table of municipalities for 2026 
into a [pandas DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html).
```{python}
import json
import requests
import pandas as pd


def load_as_df(url):
	"""Retrieve entire dataset at url and return as a dataframe"""
    # Get the first page
	resp = requests.get(url)
	resp.raise_for_status()
	resp_json = json.loads(resp.content.decode('utf-8'))
	df = pd.DataFrame(resp_json["data"])
    
    # Keep retrieving pages while there is a 'next' link
	while "next" in resp_json["links"]:
		resp = requests.get(resp_json["links"]["next"])
		resp.raise_for_status()
		resp_json = json.loads(resp.content.decode('utf-8'))
		df = pd.concat([df, pd.DataFrame(resp_json["data"])], ignore_index = True)
	return df


# Load municipality tables for 2026
municipalities_2026 = load_as_df("https://api.tor-gu.com/nj/municipalities/2026")
```
```{r echo=FALSE}
library(reticulate)
knitr::kable(head(py$municipalities_2026))
```

The `municipality_xrefs` endpoint works similarly. As an example, let's also retrieve the 
2000 municipality table along with the 2026/2000 cross-reference table, and take a look
at the changes in NJ municipalities between 2000 and 2026.
```{python comment="", strip.white=TRUE}
municipalities_2000 = load_as_df("https://api.tor-gu.com/nj/municipalities/2000")
xrefs = load_as_df("https://api.tor-gu.com/nj/municipality_xrefs/2026/2000")
# Select columns for a merged table
xrefs = xrefs.rename(
	columns={"GEOID_ref": "GEOID_2026", "GEOID": "GEOID_2000"}
	)[["GEOID_2000", "GEOID_2026"]]
municipalities_2000 = municipalities_2000.rename(
	columns={"GEOID": "GEOID_2000", "municipality": "municipality_2000"}
	)[["GEOID_2000", "county", "municipality_2000"]]
municipalities_2026 = municipalities_2026.rename(
	columns={"GEOID": "GEOID_2026", "municipality": "municipality_2026"}
	)[["GEOID_2026","municipality_2026"]]

# Create the merged table
merged = xrefs.merge(
	municipalities_2000, how="left", on="GEOID_2000").merge(
	municipalities_2026, how="left", on="GEOID_2026").fillna("NA")

# Select all changes in municipalities between 2000 and 2026
changes = merged[(merged["municipality_2000"] != merged["municipality_2026"]) | 
	(merged["GEOID_2000"] != merged["GEOID_2026"])]
```
```{r echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(py$changes)
```

## Deploying
This API is implemented as an [AWS SAM](https://aws.amazon.com/serverless/sam/) application, with its DynamoDB
tables managed separately by [Terraform](https://www.terraform.io/). A deployment has four parts:

1. The lambda layer [layer_torguapi](https://github.com/tor-gu/layer_torguapi), which needs to be deployed separately.
2. The DynamoDB tables, defined in `infra/`.
3. The data: CSV exports of the tables in [njmunicipalities](https://github.com/tor-gu/njmunicipalities), committed
   in `data/` and loaded into the tables by `scripts/load_data.py`.
4. The lambdas and API Gateway, defined in `template.yaml`.

The tables are deliberately kept out of the SAM template, so that deploying the application can never replace them.
Terraform owns the tables, and the loader owns their contents.

### Tables
Terraform state is kept in an S3 bucket, with one state file per environment (see `infra/env/*.backend.hcl`;
the bucket must exist and should be versioned). Terraform 1.10 or later is required, for S3 state locking.
```
make tf_plan ENV=dev      # review the plan, then
make tf_apply ENV=dev
```
The tables have deletion protection and point-in-time recovery enabled.

### Data
`data/` holds `counties.csv`, `municipalities.csv`, and `SOURCE`, which records the njmunicipalities release
they were exported from. To export a release (this needs R and the `remotes` package; the release is installed
into a temporary library):
```
make export_data REF=v1.4.0
```
`scripts/load_data.py` brings the tables in line with `data/`: rows that are new or changed are written, and rows
no longer in the CSVs are deleted. To preview what it would change:
```
make load_dry_run ENV=dev
```
The pipeline runs the loader on every deploy, then passes the version in `data/SOURCE` to the template's
`DataVersion` parameter. The lambdas cache the tables, and the load is not atomic, so when the version changes
the lambdas are updated, which discards anything they cached during the load.

### Annual data update
1. `make export_data REF=<new release>`, and review the diff in `data/`.
2. Update the hard-coded current year: `DEFAULT_YEAR` in `municipalities/app/municipalities_lib.py`, the examples
   in `njmunicipalities-openapi.yaml` and in this README (then `make knit`), and the unit tests.
3. `make load_dry_run ENV=dev` to preview the load.
4. Push to `dev`, check the dev API, then merge to `master`.

### Direct deploy
The application can be deployed directly using the SAM CLI. Load the data first, then deploy with the matching
`DataVersion`:
```
python scripts/load_data.py
sam build
sam deploy --stack-name MyStackName                                                         \
           --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM                                                    \
           --resolve-s3                                                                     \
           --parameter-overrides                                                            \
                TorguapiLayerArn=arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:layer:layer_torguapi \
                TorguapiLayerVersion=1                                                      \
                ApiRoot=https://api.example.com                                             \
                DataVersion=$(sed -n 's/^version=//p' data/SOURCE)
```
Replace the `TorguapiLayerXXX` params with the values derived from the `layer_torguapi` deployment.

The `ApiRoot` value is used only for generating the values in `"links"` in the JSON reply. On
`api.tor-gu.com`, the relationship between the publicly facing API URL and the API Gateway
endpoints is configured in [torgu-api-cloudfront](https://github.com/tor-gu/torgu-api-cloudfront).

To deploy a second environment alongside the first, give it a resource name prefix (I use `dev-`): set
`EnvPrefix` in the template parameters, `--env-prefix` for the loader, and `env_prefix` in `infra/env/*.tfvars`.

### Using a pipeline
The package also includes the code pipeline that I use to deploy from github. Each run updates the pipeline
itself, runs the unit tests, builds the application, loads the data, and deploys.

In addition to the requirements above, you will need to have execution roles for the
pipeline (`PipelineExecutionRole`) and for the deployment itself
(`CloudFormationExecutionRole`). The pipeline's CodeBuild role is granted read and batch-write access to the
environment's two tables, for the data load.

```
aws cloudformation deploy --stack-name MyPipelineStackName \
    --template-file codepipeline.yaml \
    --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM \
    --parameter-overrides \
        ArtifactBucket=MyArtifactBucket \
        PipelineExecutionRole=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MyPipelineExecutionRole \
        CloudFormationExecutionRole=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/MyCloudFormationExecutionRole \
        Region=us-east-1 \
        DeployStackName=MyStackName \
        TorguapiLayerArn=arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:layer:layer_torguapi \
        TorguapiLayerVersion=1 \
        ApiRoot=https://api.example.com
```
